1.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [contend against those who fight against me]

The words **oppose** and **fight** are imperatives, but they communicate polite requests rather than commands. If the imperatives do not communicate polite requests for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. Here and throughout the psalm where this form is used, it may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, please oppose my opponents; please fight those fighting me]

David is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root in both of these phrases. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [go to battle against my enemies; fight against those who are attacking me]

2.note: David is using **rise up** as a common expression of the culture to ask Yahweh to take action. He is not telling him to get out of bed or stand up from a seated position. If this expression does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [take action]

3.note: The terms **spear** and **javelin** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Draw out your weapons]

David is using the term **my soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [assure me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the one who rescues you]

4.q: יֵבֹ֣שׁוּ וְ⁠יִכָּלְמוּ֮ מְבַקְשֵׁ֪י נַ֫פְשִׁ֥⁠י יִסֹּ֣גוּ אָח֣וֹר וְ⁠יַחְפְּר֑וּ חֹ֝שְׁבֵ֗י רָעָתִֽ⁠י
4.note: In this verse and throughout the psalm, David is saying what he wants Yahweh to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do.

The expressions **have shame** and **be dishonored** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [May those who want to kill me be utterly disgraced]

David is using **seek my life** as a common expression to mean “try to kill me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who try to kill me]

The expression **be dishonored** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who did the action, it is clear from the context that it was Yahweh. Alternate translation: [and may Yahweh dishonor them]

Here David is speaking of being unable to accomplish a goal as if the enemies were walking one direction and had to **be turned back**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May those who plan my harm be unsuccessful and confused]

The expression **be turned back** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who did the action, it is clear from the context that it was Yahweh. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh cause those who plan my harm to be unsuccessful and confused]

5.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **chaff** is easily blown away by the wind, so David’s enemies will be easily scattered. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [easily scattered like chaff before the wind]

6.note: David is speaking of how his enemies live as if that were a **way** or path that they were walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May their lives be full of danger and uncertainty]

Here David is speaking of keeping the enemies from harming him as if the **angel of Yahweh** were physically running and **chasing them** away. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [keeps them from harming me]

7.q: כִּֽי־חִנָּ֣ם טָֽמְנוּ־לִ֭⁠י שַׁ֣חַת רִשְׁתָּ֑⁠ם חִ֝נָּ֗ם חָפְר֥וּ לְ⁠נַפְשִֽׁ⁠י
7.note: The phrases **they hid for me a pit, their net; without cause they dug for my life** is a translation of the written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. Scholars have proposed that a scribe may have accidentally switched the order of the words for “pit” and “their net.” Many translations put “their net” first so that “a pit” begins the second line, and you may want to do the same. Alternate translation: [For they hid for me their net; a pit without cause they dug for my life]

David is speaking of his enemies’ schemes as if they were **a pit** and a **net** used to trap animals. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they secretly plotted to trap me]

8.q: תְּבוֹאֵ֣⁠הוּ שׁוֹאָה֮ לֹֽא־יֵ֫דָ֥ע וְ⁠רִשְׁתּ֣⁠וֹ אֲשֶׁר־טָמַ֣ן תִּלְכְּד֑⁠וֹ בְּ֝⁠שׁוֹאָ֗ה יִפָּל־בָּֽ⁠הּ
8.note: Throughout this verse, the pronouns **him** and **he** are singular, but they refer to all of David’s enemies as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural forms as modeled in the UST.

David is speaking of **destruction** as if it were a living thing that could a dangerous animal that would chase the enemies down and suddenly attack them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Let them be surprised because you destroy them suddenly]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **destruction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Let him be destroyed]

David is describing the ironic reversal in which the traps his enemies prepared will instead ensnare them. The **net** they set for David will **catch** them, and they will fall to their own **destruction** into the “pit” they “dug.” If a speaker of your language would not express this reversal in this way, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Let his own trap catch him; let him fall into ruin by his own scheming]

9.note: David is using the term **my soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [But I will be joyful in Yahweh; I will rejoice]

David uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the destruction of his enemies and his own joy in Yahweh. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Despite all this, my soul will be joyful in Yahweh]

The terms **joyful** and **rejoice** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [my soul will celebrate with great gladness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that he rescued me]

10.note: David speaks of his **bones** as if they were a person who could speak. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Every part of me will declare]

David is using one part of his body, his **bones**, to represent his entire being. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Everything within me]

10.q: יְהוָ֗ה מִ֥י כָ֫מ֥וֹ⁠ךָ מַצִּ֣יל עָ֭נִי מֵ⁠חָזָ֣ק מִמֶּ֑⁠נּוּ וְ⁠עָנִ֥י וְ֝⁠אֶבְי֗וֹן מִ⁠גֹּזְלֽ⁠וֹ
10.note: David is using the question form to emphasize that no one is comparable to Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There is no one like you, Yahweh! You rescue the oppressed from those stronger than them and the oppressed and needy from those robbing them.]

David is using the adjectives **oppressed** and **needy** as nouns to mean a certain kind of person. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate these with equivalent expressions. Alternate translation: [those who are oppressed from those stronger than them and those who are oppressed and needy]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and rescuing the oppressed and needy]

11.note: David is using the possessive form to describe **Witnesses** that are characterized by **violence**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Witnesses who wish me harm rise up]

David is using **rise up** as a common expression of the culture to mean to take action. He is not saying that they get out of bed or stand up from a seated position. If this expression does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Witnesses take violent action against me]

12.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **evil** and **good**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [by doing bad things to me in place of the good things I did for them]

Here David is speaking of the way his enemies treated him as if they were paying back a loan or trying to **repay** him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They treated me with]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **bereavement**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [they have bereaved my soul]

David is using the term **my soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I feel bereaved]

13.note: David uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between his enemies’ cruelty toward him and his kindness toward them when they were sick. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I, on the other hand]

Wearing **sackcloth** was a symbolic action by which David expressed grief and mourning. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [I dressed in rough cloth as a sign of sorrow for them]

David is using the term **my soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [myself]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **fasting**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by refusing to eat]

David is using **my prayer returned upon my bosom** as a common expression of his culture to mean that he prayed sincerely, with his head bowed to his chest. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I prayed with my head bowed down]

14.q: כְּ⁠רֵֽעַ־כְּ⁠אָ֣ח לִ֭⁠י הִתְהַלָּ֑כְתִּי כַּ⁠אֲבֶל־אֵ֝֗ם קֹדֵ֥ר שַׁחֽוֹתִי
14.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [I walked about as one lamenting for a mother, as for a friend, as for a brother; mourning, I bowed down]

The point of this comparison is that just as a person would grieve for **a friend** or **a brother**, so David grieved for his enemies when they were sick. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [As if each one were my close friend or a brother, I walked about]

The point of this comparison is that just as a person in deep grief would be **lamenting** the loss of **a mother**, so David mourned deeply for his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [with grief as deep as one who has lost his mother]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [as one who was lamenting for his mother]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **mourning**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I mourned and bowed down]

The action of **bowing down** was a symbolic action by which David showed deep grief and mourning. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [I expressed deep sorrow]

15.note: David uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between his compassion for his enemies and their cruelty when he suffered. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However, at my stumbling]

David is speaking of experiencing trouble as if it were physically **stumbling**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But at my time of difficulty]
The pronoun **they** refers to David’s enemies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [my enemies rejoiced and gathered together]

The word translated as **the stricken ones** represents the written Hebrew text. This could refer to the mockers imitating David’s lameness as possibly described in verse 16, if vowels are used to read “deformity” instead of “food” in that verse. However, scholars have proposed that changing one vowel here would make the word “the strikers,” which seems to fit better the meaning of this verse. The UST follows that interpretation. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [the strikers I did not even know]

David is speaking of his enemies’ verbal attacks as if they physically **tore** at him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They attacked me with words and did not cease]

16.note: The word translated as food represents the written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. Scholars have proposed that by changing the vowels of this word it would say “deformity,” which seems to fit better the meaning of this passage. The UST follows that interpretation. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [my deformity]

**They gnashed their teeth at me** describes a symbolic action by which the enemies express rage and contempt. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [they showed their anger and hostility toward me]

17.note: David is using the question form to urgently appeal to God for help. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Lord, you have looked on long enough!]

David is using the term **my soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **destructions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the things they do to try to destroy me]

David is using **my only one** as a common expression to mean his precious, irreplaceable life. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my precious life]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [please rescue my life]

David is speaking of his enemies as if they were **young lions** that were attacking him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from these fierce enemies]

19.note: David is using **wink the eye** to show a symbolic action by which someone showed scorn or signaling conspiracy against someone else. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [let not the haters of me without cause signal their contempt]

20.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason the enemies should not rejoice over David’s suffering mentioned in the previous verses. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Since they do not speak peace]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [peaceful words]

David is speaking of peaceable people as **the quiet ones**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and against those who live quietly in the land]

David is using the adjective **quiet** as a noun to mean people who are quiet and peaceable. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this with an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [the peaceful people of the land]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **deceits**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [deceptive words]

21.note: David is using the phrase **open their mouth wide** to represent what the enemies shouted loudly. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They speak loudly against me]

David’s enemies are using **Aha, Aha,** as a phrase that expresses a strong feeling or gloating and malicious delight at the misfortune of another person. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [You did it!]

David’s enemies are using **our eyes** to represent what they have witnessed. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we have witnessed it]

22.note: David is speaking of a lack of intervention as being **silent**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [do not remain inactive]

David is speaking of a lack of help as being physically **far** from him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [do not withhold your help from me]

23.note: David is speaking of God as if he were sleeping and needed to **Awake** or **arouse** himself from sleep. He means that he is asking God to act on his behalf and intervene in this situation. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Take action] or [I ask you to intervene]

The expressions **Awake** and **arouse yourself** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Rouse yourself fully]

The terms **my justice** and **my cause** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [to come to my defense, my God and my Lord]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for you to judge me fairly]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **cause**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to defend me against my accusers]

24.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [according to the right way that you judge]

25.q: אַל־יֹאמְר֣וּ בְ֭⁠לִבָּ⁠ם הֶאָ֣ח נַפְשֵׁ֑⁠נוּ אַל־יֹ֝אמְר֗וּ בִּֽלַּעֲנֽוּ⁠הוּ
25.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could express these as indirect quotations. Alternate translation: [Do not let them think that they have gotten what they desire. Do not let them say that they have destroyed me]

David is using **say in their heart** as a common expression of the culture to mean “say to themselves.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do not let them say to themselves]

The exclamation **Aha** expresses the enemies’ malicious gloating. The phrase **our soul** in this context means “we have gotten what we desired” which is to have him be declared guilty. Your language may have a comparable exclamation that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Hurrah! Our wish has been fulfilled] or [We are so glad he has been declared guilty just as we desired]

David’s enemies are speaking of defeating him completely as if they were wild animals who had **swallowed him up**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [We have totally overcome him]

26.note: The expressions **be ashamed** and **confounded** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [be completely put to shame together]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [at my misfortune]

David is speaking of **shame and humiliation** as if these were garments that his enemies would wear or **be clothed** in. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [be completely covered in disgrace]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **shame** and **humiliation**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Let them be completely ashamed and humiliated]

The expression **be clothed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [May God clothe them]

The terms **shame** and **humiliation** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [with utter disgrace]

David is using **magnifying themselves against me** as a common expression to mean boasting or exalting themselves in defiance of him. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who exalt themselves over me]

27.note: The expressions **shout for joy** and **be glad** mean similar things. David is using the two expressions together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Let them greatly rejoice]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [my being declared right]

27.q: וְ⁠יֹאמְר֣וּ תָ֭מִיד יִגְדַּ֣ל יְהוָ֑ה הֶ֝⁠חָפֵ֗ץ שְׁל֣וֹם עַבְדּֽ⁠וֹ
27.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as an indirect quotation. Alternate translation: [and let them continually declare that Yahweh is great, the one delighting in the peace of his servant]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **word**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the welfare of]

28.note: The word translated as **And** connects this verse to what came before as a result. David is saying that because Yahweh will act on his behalf, he will respond with praise. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [Because of this, my tongue will meditate on your righteousness]

David is using one part of his person, his **tongue**, to mean all of him in the act of meditating. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [For I will speak about]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the ways you act righteously]

David is saying **all the day** as an overstatement to emphasize that his praise will be constant and habitual. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [continually]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **praise**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [praising you]
